implementation_notes: The Kafka client is a polling consumer by design: poll(Duration) returns a bounded batch (max.poll.records), returns an empty batch when nothing arrives within the timeout, and doubles as the group heartbeat, so the poll interval is a liveness parameter (max.poll.interval.ms) as much as a throughput one. Acknowledgement is the offset commit and belongs after processing - enable.auto.commit acknowledges at poll time and loses messages when the process dies between the poll and the work.
pitfalls: poll(Duration) is also the liveness heartbeat: a batch that takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms to process evicts the consumer from its group, and the next commit fails with CommitFailedException.

Auto-commit acknowledges records as poll() returns them, so a crash before the work silently loses them; disabling it and committing after processing makes the receiver at-least-once and requires idempotent handlers.
KafkaConsumer is not thread-safe: keep one poll loop per consumer and use wakeup() for shutdown instead of sharing the consumer across threads.

variants.name: JMS synchronous receiver (receive/receiveNoWait)
variants.implementation_notes: The EIP-era realization: the consumer calls MessageConsumer.receive(timeout), which blocks at most timeout milliseconds and returns null when it expires, or receiveNoWait() for the immediate variant - exactly the receive/receiveNoWait pair the pattern describes. Acknowledgement is the JMS acknowledgement mode or the transaction: in a transacted session the message is retained until commit, so a crash rolls it back to the queue, whereas a non-transacted AUTO_ACKNOWLEDGE session acknowledges on delivery, that is, before the work happens.
pitfalls: receive(0) means 'block indefinitely' rather than 'return immediately'; the immediate answer is receiveNoWait(), and a zero timeout in a poll loop hangs the consumer instead of polling it.

AUTO_ACKNOWLEDGE acknowledges on delivery, so a failure during handling loses the message; a transacted session or CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE is required when the acknowledgement point must follow processing.

variants.name: Virtual-thread consumer with blocking receive (Loom)
variants.implementation_notes: With virtual threads the polling consumer returns to its simplest form: one virtual thread per consumer runs an ordinary blocking receive with a timeout, and because a blocked virtual thread unmounts from its carrier the thread-per-consumer cost that motivated batching and callback plumbing largely disappears. The pattern's responsibilities do not move - timeout, idle policy, acknowledgement and shutdown are still the consumer's - but the code can be written as a plain loop, which makes this variant preferable on Java 21+ for many low-to-moderate-volume channels.
pitfalls: Virtual threads do not make polling cheaper on the wire: one thread per channel still issues one idle fetch per interval, so the fan-out limit is the channel's capacity, not the thread's cost.
A blocked thread that pins its carrier (inside a synchronized block or a native frame) behaves like a platform thread under load and loses the scalability this variant was chosen for.
